description: The Deported Veterans Support House in Tijuana - 'the Bunker' - was founded in 2013 by Hector Barajas, a deported former 82nd Airborne paratrooper, after he began meeting homeless deported US veterans in the city. It is part shelter, part advocacy office, in a two-storey building attached to a tyre shop, with portraits of deported servicemen up the staircase.
energy_note: A shelter for men who served, run by one of them.

description: 'We call it the Bunker here because ... this is kind of like ... our place for us to be safe.'
energy_note: Safe, in the country they were sent to.

aspect: EXAMPLE - the scale is unknown and the known cases are many
description: Barajas estimated around 40 veterans had passed through the Bunker by 2016; by 2017 he had identified 350 deported US veterans born in more than 30 countries. Advocates believe there may be thousands worldwide. No government publishes the number.

aspect: The belief that service conferred citizenship
description: Many at the Bunker said that when they enlisted they were led to believe naturalisation would be automatic. Most came to the US as children and were lawful permanent residents when they served.
energy_note: He thought the uniform had already made him one.

aspect: EXAMPLE - a pardon is what it took
description: Barajas was able to become a US citizen only after a pardon from California Governor Jerry Brown in 2018. He later helped open a support house in the Dominican Republic.
energy_note: It took a governor's pardon to undo it.

aspect: Benefits he is still owed, in a country he cannot enter
description: VA healthcare entitlements frequently survive removal in principle while being unreachable in practice, since receiving them requires being in the United States.
energy_note: Entitled to care he would have to break the law to collect.

description: The Bunker is decorated with US flags and portraits of deported servicemen in uniform, with medals, discharge papers and photographs collaged on the walls - men asserting an allegiance to a country that has formally removed them.
energy_note: Saluting a flag that deported him.

description: Deported veterans frequently remain eligible for burial in a US national cemetery - so the state that would not let them live there will accept them once dead. This is the single most quotable fact in the dataset.
energy_note: Allowed back across the line in a coffin.
